headline: MP Gazi Nazrul's second wife found dead, case filed against him and two others
summary: Mariam Khatun's hanging body was recovered from a NAM Bhaban flat in Dhaka. Her father has filed a case of abetment to death against MP Gazi Nazrul, his first wife, and her maternal uncle.
details: A case has been filed against Satkhira-4 MP Gazi Nazrul Islam and two others on charges of abetting the death of his second wife, Mariam Khatun. Mariam's hanging body was recovered from a flat at NAM Bhaban in Dhaka last night.

Mariam's father, Masum Billah, filed the case with Sher-e-Bangla Nagar Police Station late Sunday night. Gazi Nazrul's first wife, Maksuda Begum, and Mariam's maternal uncle Obaidur Rahman were also named as accused.
Police stated that Gazi Nazrul was present at the flat when Mariam's body was recovered. Following this, he and Maksuda were taken to the police station for questioning.

Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Ibne Mizan clarified that Gazi Nazrul has not been arrested in the case. As a lawmaker, he is subject to specific legal procedures before an arrest can be shown, but questioning is ongoing.

headline: 36 missing children's bodies recovered in 8 months, 26 killed after rape; community safety net failing
summary: The tragic death of a Comilla University teacher's son highlights a disturbing trend of missing children and juvenile delinquency. Experts point to a breakdown in traditional community safety nets and a reliance on an inadequate formal policing system.
details: The tragic death of Ishiat Shahriar Opratim, a 13-year-old son of a Comilla University teacher, is part of a disturbing trend. Between January and July this year, 15,717 children were reported missing, with 36 bodies recovered in eight months and 26 killed after rape.

Opratim's case, allegedly involving teenagers, has brought juvenile delinquency into sharp focus. Disappearances among teens are often linked to emotional distress, academic pressures, family disputes, and peer influence, compounded by a desire for independence and a breakdown in societal values.

Historically, Bangladeshi communities relied on an "endogenous security framework." This organic system was built on mutual surveillance, shared social responsibility, and deep empathy, especially in traditional rural and semi-urban neighborhoods where people actively looked out for one another's children.

However, rapid urbanization and neoliberal economic structures have dismantled this internal resilience. Neoliberalism, emphasizing individual achievement and market competition, has shifted Bangladesh away from community-centric living towards extreme individualism and hyper-competition.

This cultural shift has severely eroded collective empathy, replacing traditional social vigilance with indifference in urban areas. People are less likely to intervene when a child is in distress, creating an environment ripe for exploitation by criminals, local gangs, and kidnappers.

Further fragmentation is caused by intense political division and economic polarization. Political patronage and factionalism fracture communities, hindering collective action, while the desperate pursuit of material status drives young people into precarious situations, fueling delinquency and violence.

As the traditional security mechanism crumbles, society increasingly relies on an "exogenous security system" – formal policing, state surveillance, and legal frameworks. However, this system is profoundly mismatched with the structural reality of Bangladeshi communities.

Unlike advanced nations with massive technological infrastructure and well-equipped, politically independent police forces, Bangladesh's state machinery lacks the capacity, technology, and manpower. It cannot effectively monitor every alleyway or protect every citizen in a densely populated, resource-constrained environment.
